title: Coastal Wholesale: analyzing a customer's credit application
participant_role: Credit analyst at a food service distributor reviewing a new customer's credit application
judge_role: Sales manager of Coastal Wholesale, who is eager to approve a $50,000 credit line for Bayside Cafe Group

difficulty.rationale: Four ratios vs industry and a credit decision.

scenario:
You are to assume the role of credit analyst for COASTAL WHOLESALE, a distributor of food, beverages and paper goods to restaurants. The sales manager (judge) wants you to approve a credit application from a new customer.

BAYSIDE CAFE GROUP operates six cafes and wants to buy its supplies from COASTAL WHOLESALE on account. Bayside has asked for a $50,000 line of credit on 30-day terms. The sales manager (judge) is eager to approve the application because Bayside could become one of the region's largest accounts. The sales manager (judge) told you, "They run six busy cafes. Just approve it so we can ship the first order on Monday."

Company policy requires the credit department to review every new credit line over $10,000. Bayside provided its most recent financial statements, and you found industry averages for restaurant groups in a trade association report. You also searched the company's customer relationship management (CRM) system and learned that Bayside bought from another COASTAL WHOLESALE division last year.

[Bayside financial data: see exhibits]

[Industry averages: see exhibits]

[CRM record: see exhibits]

The sales manager (judge) needs a clear decision to take back to Bayside this week and does not want to lose the account or damage the relationship.

You must:
- Explain why credit matters to both COASTAL WHOLESALE and Bayside
- Analyze Bayside's financial information
- Use the CRM data to evaluate Bayside's payment history
- Recommend and negotiate a credit decision
- Explain how CRM and database tools can support future credit decisions

You will present your recommendation to the sales manager (judge) in a role-play to take place in the sales manager's (judge's) office. The sales manager (judge) will begin the role-play by greeting you and asking to hear your ideas. After you have presented your recommendation and have answered the sales manager's (judge's) questions, the sales manager (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your work.
tasks: Explain why credit matters to both COASTAL WHOLESALE and Bayside
Use the CRM data to evaluate Bayside's payment history
Recommend and negotiate a credit decision
Explain how CRM and database tools can support future credit decisions

judge_questions: If we say no, they'll buy from our competitor. Isn't some sales better than none?
What would change your mind in six months?

solution.overview: A strong answer explains why trade credit helps both sides, then shows that Bayside is weaker than the industry on every ratio (current ratio 1.2, quick ratio 0.53, debt ratio 80%, net margin 2%) and pays about 15 days late. The presenter recommends a smaller, conditional line (for example $20,000) or cash on delivery instead of the full $50,000, negotiates respectfully to keep the customer, and explains how CRM and database tools give one view of each customer's payment history.

answer: For COASTAL WHOLESALE, offering credit helps win and keep customers and increases sales
Every credit sale is a risk: if Bayside does not pay, COASTAL loses the cost of the goods and its profit, and cash is tied up while it waits
For Bayside, credit lets it buy supplies now and pay after it earns revenue, which helps its cash flow
A good payment record builds Bayside's credit reputation and can earn it a larger line later
Current ratio: 180,000 / 150,000 = 1.2, below the industry 1.5, so less ability to pay short-term bills
Quick ratio: (30,000 + 50,000) / 150,000 = 0.53, below 0.8, because much of its current assets is inventory
Debt ratio: 400,000 / 500,000 = 80%, above 60%, so Bayside already relies heavily on borrowed money
Net profit margin: 18,000 / 900,000 = 2%, half the industry 4%, leaving little cushion if sales slow
Other checks: credit bureau report, trade references and bank references (the five Cs of credit)
Bayside paid in 45 days on 30-day terms, about 15 days late on average
Two sales rep notes confirm repeated late payment and broken promises
Past payment behavior with our own company is one of the best predictors of future behavior
The ratios and the payment history point the same way: higher than normal credit risk

by_task.task: Recommend and negotiate a credit decision
answer: Do not approve the full $50,000 line now
Offer a smaller line (for example $20,000) with conditions such as a personal guarantee or deposit and shorter terms, or offer cash on delivery
Review the account after 6 months of on-time payments and raise the limit if earned
Negotiate respectfully: thank Bayside for its business, explain the path to a larger line and look for a win for both sides
A single customer record across all divisions shows orders, payment history and notes in one place
Set automatic alerts for late payers and link credit limits to order entry so orders over the limit are held
Run database queries and reports, for example all customers paying more than 30 days past terms
Share credit data with sales so reps know a customer's status before promising terms

judge_question_answers.question: If we say no, they'll buy from our competitor. Isn't some sales better than none?
answer: Sales only help if we get paid; an unpaid $50,000 balance wipes out the profit on many other orders
We are not saying no: a smaller, secured line or cash on delivery still lets us win the business
If Bayside proves it pays on time, we can raise the limit
A competitor that gives full credit is taking on the risk we are avoiding

judge_question_answers.question: What would change your mind in six months?
answer: Six months of payments within 30 days on the smaller line
Improved financial statements: a current ratio closer to 1.5 and less debt
Better profit margin and a clean credit bureau and bank reference
With that record we would gladly consider raising the line toward $50,000

key_concepts.definition: The ability to buy goods or services now and pay for them later, based on trust that payment will be made.
The maximum amount a supplier allows a customer to owe on account at one time, with set payment terms such as net 30.
Current assets divided by current liabilities. Measures ability to pay short-term debts.
Cash plus receivables (and short-term investments) divided by current liabilities. A stricter liquidity test that leaves out inventory.
Total liabilities divided by total assets. Shows how much of the business is financed with debt.
Net income divided by sales. Shows how much profit is earned on each sales dollar.
Character, capacity, capital, collateral and conditions: the factors lenders and credit managers use to judge a borrower.
Technology that stores and organizes all information about customers, such as contacts, orders, payments and notes.
A request that pulls specific records from a database, such as all customers more than 30 days past due.
A promise by a business owner to pay the business's debt personally if the business does not.
Discussion aimed at reaching an agreement that meets the needs of both sides.

notes: State level because the ratios are standard and the key skill is linking them to CRM history and a firm but friendly recommendation. Watch for students who include inventory in the quick ratio, who simply approve or deny without conditions, or who forget to keep the customer relationship positive.

items.label: Describe techniques used to analyze customer financial information

criteria.exceeds: Calculates and compares all four ratios with the industry: current ratio 1.2 against 1.5, quick ratio 0.53 against 0.8, debt ratio 80% against 60% and net profit margin 2% against 4%, explains what each weakness means for Bayside's ability to pay, and mentions other checks such as credit bureau, trade and bank references (the five Cs of credit).
criteria.meets: Correctly calculates the current ratio 1.2, quick ratio 0.53, debt ratio 80% and net margin 2% and states that Bayside is weaker than the industry on each.
criteria.below: Calculates only some ratios, or makes an error such as including inventory in the quick ratio (giving 1.2), or computes ratios without comparing them to the industry.
criteria.little: Does not analyze the financial statements, or the numbers are unrelated to the exhibit.

criteria.exceeds: Uses the CRM record to show Bayside paid in 45 days on 30-day terms, about 15 days late on average, cites both sales rep notes (two past due calls in March and a check 10 days after the promised date), and explains that past payment behavior with our own company is one of the best predictors and points the same way as the ratios.
criteria.meets: Uses the CRM data to show Bayside pays about 15 days late and has a history of past due invoices.
criteria.below: Mentions the CRM record but does not calculate the 15 days late or ignores the rep notes.
criteria.little: Does not use the CRM data.

criteria.exceeds: Recommends a single customer record across all divisions, automatic late payer alerts, credit limits linked to order entry so orders over the limit are held, database queries such as all customers paying more than 30 days past terms, and sharing credit data with sales before terms are promised.
criteria.meets: Explains at least two ways CRM and database tools can support credit decisions, such as a shared customer record, alerts or queries of late payers.
criteria.below: Says the CRM is useful in general terms without specific features or reports.
criteria.little: Does not explain how CRM or database tools could help.

items.label: Explain the purposes and importance of credit

criteria.exceeds: Explains that credit helps COASTAL WHOLESALE win customers and grow sales but risks the cost of goods, profit and tied up cash if Bayside does not pay, and that for Bayside credit supports cash flow and a good payment record builds its reputation toward a larger line.
criteria.meets: Explains why credit matters to both the seller and the buyer, including the risk of nonpayment.
criteria.below: Explains credit from only one side, or does not mention the risk to COASTAL WHOLESALE.
criteria.little: Does not explain the purpose or importance of credit.

criteria.exceeds: Declines the full $50,000 line but offers a smaller conditional line (for example $20,000) with a personal guarantee or deposit and shorter terms, or cash on delivery, with a 6-month review to raise the limit, and presents it respectfully so the sales manager and Bayside see a win for both sides.
criteria.meets: Recommends a smaller or conditional line instead of the full $50,000 and suggests a path to a larger line while keeping the relationship positive.
criteria.below: Simply approves or denies the $50,000 without conditions or alternatives, or delivers the decision in a way that could damage the relationship.
criteria.little: Approves the full $50,000 because the sales manager wants it, or gives no recommendation.

items.label: Critical Thinking: Reason effectively and use systems thinking

criteria.exceeds: Connects the weak ratios, the 15 days late history and company policy into one credit risk picture, and weighs the sales opportunity against the cost of an unpaid balance.
criteria.meets: Reasons correctly from the financial data and CRM history to a higher than normal credit risk.
criteria.below: Reaches a conclusion without showing the reasoning, or looks at only the ratios or only the history.

items.label: Problem Solving: Make judgments and decisions and solve problems

criteria.exceeds: Gives a clear, conditional decision the sales manager can take to Bayside this week, with specific terms and a review date that protects COASTAL while keeping the first order on track.
criteria.meets: Makes a clear recommendation for a smaller, conditional line or cash on delivery.
criteria.below: Hesitates, or gives a recommendation that is partly correct or not clearly stated.
criteria.little: Makes no recommendation, or ignores the risk.

criteria.exceeds: Explains the ratios and payment history in plain language a sales manager can follow, stays firm but friendly, and delivers confidently and professionally.
criteria.meets: Presents the analysis and recommendation clearly and in an organized way.
criteria.below: Presentation is hard to follow, relies on jargon, or sounds dismissive of the sales goal.

items.label: Creativity and Innovation: Show evidence of creativity

criteria.exceeds: Uses a side by side table of Bayside against the industry averages and designs creative terms, such as a starter line that grows with on-time payments, that help both companies.
criteria.meets: Organizes the information in a way that makes the recommendation easy to understand.
criteria.below: Presents the facts with little effort to make them engaging or easy to follow.
criteria.little: Shows no evidence of creativity or original thought.

items.label: Overall impression and responses to the judge's questions

criteria.exceeds: Answers both questions correctly and confidently: sales only help if we get paid and an unpaid $50,000 wipes out the profit on many orders, but a smaller secured line or cash on delivery still wins the business and a competitor giving full credit takes the risk; and six months of payments within 30 days, a current ratio closer to 1.5, less debt, a better margin and clean references would support raising the line toward $50,000.
criteria.meets: Answers both questions mostly correctly, including that the conditional offer still keeps the sale and that on-time payments and better ratios would earn a larger line.
criteria.below: Answers only one question correctly, or gives vague answers without specific conditions.
criteria.little: Cannot answer the judge's questions, or agrees that any sale is better than none regardless of risk.

key_points: Quick ratio: (30,000 + 50,000) / 150,000 = 0.53, below the industry 0.8 (inventory is excluded)
Debt ratio: 400,000 / 500,000 = 80%, above the industry 60%; net profit margin: 18,000 / 900,000 = 2%, half the industry 4%
CRM: Bayside paid in 45 days on 30-day terms, about 15 days late, with notes of past due calls and a late check
Do not approve the full $50,000; offer a smaller conditional line (for example $20,000) with a guarantee or deposit and shorter terms, or cash on delivery
Review after 6 months of on-time payments and raise the limit if earned, keeping the relationship positive
CRM and database tools: one customer record across divisions, late payer alerts, credit limits linked to order entry and queries of slow payers
